newsitem.title: UK: Labour supports Cook after marriage split-up.
newsitem.headline: Labour supports Cook after marriage split-up.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook's decision to leave his wife of 28 years for his parliamentary secretary on Sunday sparked a row over what the opposition called double standards in politics.
Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair stood by Cook, insisting that the breakup was a strictly personal matter that would in no way affect Cook's high-profile job.
But the Conservative opposition party, drummed out of office in the May 1 election after being hit by a string of sexual and financial scandals, angrily accused Labour's leaders of hypocrisy.
The bearded Cook, who has been travelling almost constantly from Hong Kong to Bosnia since becoming foreign secretary, looked grave and ashen-faced when announcing his marriage was over.

The 51-year-old Cook told reporters outside his London office on Saturday night that he was leaving his 50-year-old wife Margaret, a consultant haematologist, for Gaynor Regan, 41, who has been his parliamentary aide for the past five years.
"While I accept that I am a figure in public life, I would ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this very painful time," he said.
His announcement followed revelations of the affair carried on the front page of the tabloid News of the World. The Cooks have two grown-up sons.
Conservative Party vice-chairman Alan Duncan locked horns with Labour's influential minister without portfolio Peter Mandelson over Cook's marriage breakup.

Duncan told GMTV: "Whenever it was a Conservative minister in a similar predicament, the likes of Peter Mandelson would get a lot of people to do their dirty work, to try to condemn it and cause us embarrassment.
"I hope now from this point that these double standards on the part of Labour politicians like Peter Mandelson can come to an end, that he can apologise for what he did."
Duncan himself quit as a ministerial aide in January 1994 after buying a cut-price local council house.
Mandelson, one of the chief architects of Labour's landslide victory against a party weighed down with sleaze allegations, rejected Duncan's claims.
"Labour has never made any comment, never exploited any personal tragedy of this sort in the past. We have not done so and we don't intend to start now," he said.
On the end of Cook's marriage, he would only say: "It is a source of great personal sadness but that's the word: personal."
Blair took time out from his summer holiday in Italy with his family to say that he looked on the split as a personal tragedy.
But he insisted through a spokesman that it "does not affect Robin Cook's capability as a truly outstanding Foreign Secretary."
Blair, a practising Christian, has always been reluctant to preach to people about their private lives, insisting he has no desire to "return to the age of Victorian hypocrisy about sex."
